findings.title: Retry counter relies on a broker-incremented attribute the worker never updates
findings.evidence: attempts is computed as the parsed delivery_count plus one, but on the retry branch the code only calls queue.nack(message) and never rewrites delivery_count, so the next delivery is only counted if the broker happens to mutate that application-level attribute.
findings.recommendation: Do not depend on broker-side mutation of an application attribute. Either increment delivery_count yourself before nacking (e.g. re-send/nack with delivery_count=str(attempts)) or use the broker's native receive-count field. Also add a test with a queue whose nack re-queues the message unchanged to prove MAX_ATTEMPTS is actually reached and the message is dead-lettered rather than retried forever.

findings.title: Best-effort attempt reader does not tolerate None/missing attributes
findings.evidence: The helper only catches TypeError and ValueError; if message.attributes is None (or lacks .get) an AttributeError escapes and is not caught, since the helper is called at line 29 outside any try block, crashing process_messages for every consumer invocation. The same None attributes would also break the attribute spread in the DLQ send path.
findings.recommendation: Broaden the guard to except (TypeError, ValueError, AttributeError) or read attributes defensively (attrs = getattr(message, 'attributes', None) or {}), and use that same safe dict when spreading attributes into dlq.send. Depends on the queue returning None attributes, which is broker-dependent.

findings.title: Unguarded ack can crash the worker and duplicate DLQ entries
findings.evidence: After a successful dlq.send the code calls queue.ack(message) with no try/except; if the ack raises, the exception propagates out of process_messages, the counters are never returned, and the message (already in the DLQ) is un-acked in the source queue, so it will be redelivered and dead-lettered a second time. The success-path ack at line 57 has the same uncaught-exception exposure.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the ack calls defensively (log and continue/return rather than crash) and make the DLQ send idempotent (e.g. a message id used as dedupe key) so a post-send ack failure cannot create duplicate dead-letter entries.

findings.title: DLQ send failure can spin or halt the consumer while leaving messages stranded
findings.evidence: On a persistent dlq.send failure the message is deliberately left un-acked and the loop continues; with a queue that redelivers immediately this becomes a hot retry loop against the failing DLQ, and with a queue that keeps the message in-flight the following queue.receive() can return None and break the loop, ending the worker early while the poison message is left un-acked and later messages are never processed.
findings.recommendation: On DLQ send failure, stop consuming rather than spin: break out (or apply bounded backoff with a retry cap) so the process does not busy-loop or silently terminate leaving the message un-acked, and surface the failure in the returned outcome.
